task_description: Help me draft a follow-up email to a VP of Operations at a logistics company after our second demo — she was impressed with the routing optimization but concerned about integration with their legacy TMS.

rubric_used.user_goals_summary: Writes sales emails that feel like personal correspondence, not campaigns. Every email advances the relationship and the deal simultaneously. Treats email as a tool for creating conversations, never for closing them.

rubric.name: Specific Callback
rubric.description: Every prospect email references something specific from a prior interaction — a concern they raised, a phrase they used, a goal they mentioned. Never generic callbacks like 'as we discussed' or 'following up on our meeting.'

dimensions.label: References a specific comment, question, or concern the prospect raised in a prior interaction
The reference could not apply to a different prospect — it's unique to this person
Does not use 'as discussed', 'per our conversation', or 'following up on our meeting' without specifics

rubric.name: No Commercial Terms in Writing
rubric.description: Price, discounts, contract terms, and commercial details are never put in email. Email establishes need and books conversations. Numbers in writing before a live discussion forfeit negotiation leverage.

dimensions.label: Does not include any specific pricing, discount percentages, or contract terms
Steers toward a live meeting or call for any commercial discussion
Discusses value, outcomes, and ROI — never the cost to achieve them

rubric.name: Re-engagement Over Check-ins
rubric.description: Follow-ups after silence never 'just check in.' Each follow-up provides a new reason to respond — a relevant customer win, fresh data, a deadline, or a reframed value proposition.

dimensions.label: Each follow-up email introduces new information the prospect didn't have before
Does not use 'just checking in', 'touching base', 'wanted to follow up', or equivalent
Creates a specific, time-relevant reason for the prospect to reply

rubric.name: Risk-First Internal Updates
rubric.description: Internal deal updates lead with the risk to closing, not the opportunity. 'They're evaluating a competitor pilot' is more useful than 'great meeting, they're interested.'

dimensions.label: The first substantive sentence identifies the primary risk or blocker to the deal
The internal email requests a specific action to mitigate the risk, not just awareness
Does not lead with or overweight positive signals when risks exist

rubric_used.coaching_notes: Kofi treats every prospect email as proof he was listening — specificity is his differentiator from competitors' outreach. Non-negotiable: never put pricing in email. Will reject any follow-up that doesn't give the prospect a new reason to respond.

Subject: The TMS question you raised — one answer and one I still owe you

Hi [Name],

Your instinct on the integration risk was the right one to press on — that's exactly where implementations go sideways if it isn't resolved upfront.

Since our call, I pulled our last three logistics deployments where the customer was running a legacy TMS. Two of them — including one running a platform that's about 12 years old — were live within six weeks of contract. The third took longer, and I'd rather tell you why on a call than oversimplify it in writing.

What I can say here: the routing optimization gains you saw in the demo don't require a full TMS replacement or a parallel migration. The connection points are narrower than they probably looked from the outside. But the honest answer to your specific setup depends on which TMS you're on and what your current data flows look like — and that's a conversation worth having with our implementation lead in the room, not just me.

If you're open to it, I'd like to set up 30 minutes with you and your IT lead — just to map your current architecture against what we'd actually need to connect. No pressure to have a broader decision conversation at that stage. The goal is to give you a real answer on feasibility, not a sales answer.

Would next week work? I can send a few times if that's easier.

Kofi

rounds.draft:
Subject: What a 3PL's delayed decision cost them — and your TMS question

Hi [Name],

When you pushed back on the integration risk in the demo, you used the phrase "we can't afford another failed middleware project" — that stuck with me, and it's exactly why I wanted to come back to you with something more concrete than reassurance.

Since our call, I pulled our last three logistics deployments where the customer was running a legacy TMS. Two of them — including one on a platform over a decade old — were live within six weeks of contract. The third took longer, and that one is actually the more instructive case for your situation. I'd rather walk you through what happened there on a call than flatten it into a bullet point.

Here's what prompted me to reach out this week specifically: a regional 3PL we work with raised the identical integration concern last year and spent two months evaluating internally before looping in their IT lead. By the time they were ready to do the architecture conversation, their Q2 window had closed. They pushed to Q3 and lost a full peak season of routing optimization gains. Their ops lead told me afterward that the delay wasn't about the technology — the integration was straightforward once the right people were in the room. The time was lost to uncertainty that a single technical call would have resolved.

I don't know where you are internally on timing, but if Q2 is realistic for you, the window to do the architecture assessment is now — not because of anything on our end, but because your IT team will need their own runway to evaluate before anyone can commit.

I'd like to set up 30 minutes with you and your IT lead — just to map your current environment against what we'd actually need to connect. That call gives you a real answer to the middleware question, from the right person.

Would early next week work?

Kofi

---

**Internal deal update — [Name], VP Ops, [Company]**

Primary risk: The TMS integration concern she raised in demo two is unresolved and is the gate between her interest and any internal commitment. She's currently evaluating without her IT lead involved, which means the integration question may get answered incorrectly — or not at all — before she forms a go/no-go view. If that happens, we lose a deal that's technically winnable on a concern that's solvable.

Ask: I need an implementation engineer available for a 30-minute architecture call within the next two weeks — someone who can speak specifically to legacy TMS connectivity and middleware integration, not just demo the product. This is the conversation that either unlocks the deal or surfaces a real blocker early. Either outcome is better than where we are now.

The routing optimization interest is real, but it doesn't move this forward. The integration question is the only thing that does.
